content: The European Union's Environmental Noise Directive (END) uses specific noise indicators to assess and manage environmental noise. Direct damage to the auditory system can result in hearing loss and tinnitus. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the European Commission (EC) have quantified the public health burden of environmental noise in terms of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). In Western Europe, environmental noise is estimated to result in the loss of over one million healthy life years annually, primarily due to sleep disturbances and annoyance caused by road traffic noise. Other health impacts include ischemic heart disease, cognitive impairment in children, and tinnitus. However, data gaps in Central and Eastern Europe prevent a comprehensive assessment of the entire region. The EU has been working on harmonized noise policies for decades. The Fifth Environmental Action Programme in 1993 emphasized that no individual should be exposed to noise levels that endanger health or quality of life. This was followed by the adoption of the END in 2002, which aims to prevent or reduce harmful effects of environmental noise, including annoyance. The WHO's Environmental Noise Guidelines for the European Region serve as a reference for policymakers, researchers, and advocacy groups. They exclude occupational and industrial noise, as these are regulated by workplace standards. While indoor noise levels are not explicitly addressed, they can be estimated based on outdoor levels, with typical reductions of 10–25 decibels depending on window conditions. Public perception surveys in Europe highlight significant concern about noise pollution, with many individuals reporting noise as a major issue affecting their health and well-being. Road traffic noise is the most commonly cited source of annoyance, followed by neighbor and aircraft noise. These guidelines are intended to guide policymakers and stakeholders in reducing the public health burden of noise pollution.
